name: Priya Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. This is confidential. What happens during your shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Priya, 58, and I've run the capper on a drinks bottling line for eleven years. My vocational machine-operations certificate got me in; I can tell from a crooked seal and the sound of the chuck when a batch needs stopping. I'm an experienced operator, though I still call the mechanic for a complicated fault.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What are your household finances and your experience with AI?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Dev has part-time shop hours, and our grown children pay their own way. My rate is low for an operator, there is less than a month's expenses saved, and few other bottling jobs nearby. I use AI now and then to read a maintenance notice, only after a mechanic checks the instruction. I support the union asking for paid training and safe staffing; I cannot yet put a retirement date against our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the shift that a quicker sales forecast is fine, but the bottle cap must still hold pressure. The union should see any new production target before someone is told to run the capper faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office change does not threaten my machine hours yet, but our low rate and almost empty savings make an ordinary bad week hard. Dev's shop hours vary, so I cannot rely on them to fill a hole. I feel the price of groceries before I hear much about AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep checking torque samples and stop a crooked-seal run as I do now. At the next union meeting I would ask the delegate to get the revised line target and staffing in writing; if a full paid month leaves anything after bills, I would save that new amount.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, even with the capper still needed. A faster spreadsheet does not put money in our cupboard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What tells you a seal is wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A loose cap makes a slight click when I twist the test bottle, and the torque reading confirms it. If I ignore that sound, cases can leave with leaking bottles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the union meeting achieve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I want our delegate to ask who set the new output target and whether a second operator remains on the line. It is a real meeting next week, not a petition I have only imagined.

say: I would insist the **cap seal** matters more than a faster forecast.
The **union delegate** should see any changed line target.
think: My **low wage** and thin savings make even normal bills tight.
Dev's **variable shop hours** cannot guarantee a replacement income.
do: **Keep** testing cap torque and stopping crooked seals.
**Raise** the written staffing and target question at next week's union meeting.
**Save** a new amount only after a full paid month leaves money after bills.
feel: **Uneasy** about baseline finances even while physical capper work continues.
S0.quote: A faster spreadsheet does not put money in our cupboard.
fieldNote: Her **bottling skill** remains useful in the office-first picture, while low pay and less than one month's savings already strain her budget.
She plans a **specific union meeting** about staffing and saves only fresh wage surplus, if any exists.

steps.text: Keep testing cap torque and stopping bad seals
Ask union delegate at next meeting for written targets and staffing
Save new full-month wage surplus only after bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI can reorder caps before a robot can lift a jammed bottle off my belt. If the plant wants a vision camera, the union should be shown its reject rate and any proposed hours cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A camera might make the line easier, but management could use it to run with one fewer operator. On our low pay, losing a shift would mean missing a bill; there is hardly a reserve behind us. I would try a proven display on a paid supervised shift, not a sales pitch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the union delegate to request the proposed roster and a guarded paid camera trial. If the trial is offered, I would learn the new AI reject screen by comparing marked scrap bottles with pressure and torque tests beside the mechanic. If paid hours are cut, I would apply to posted safe local production jobs only where the base wage after travel and shift times covers our bills; there are few such postings, so I would keep any available paid shifts meanwhile.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I can learn the display, but learning it will not pay rent if the roster loses a day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you put through the test?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One loose cap, one split cap and one good sealed bottle, all from a scrap run. The mechanic would guard the line while I compare each screen mark with a torque check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if a nearby job advert offers a bonus?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for the guaranteed base rate and the actual shift pattern. A bonus on a notice is no help if the bus fare and missing hours leave us short.

say: The **camera reject rate** and proposed roster belong in union talks.
A guarded **scrap trial** should compare screen marks with torque checks.
think: One lost **paid shift** would strain bills on our lower wage.
A thin **cash reserve** gives little time to find another local job.
do: **Request** the roster and a paid guarded trial through the union delegate.
**Learn** the new AI reject screen only if a supervised trial is offered.
**Apply** after cuts to posted safe local production work at bill-covering net pay.
feel: **Anxious** about a plausible shift loss despite willingness to learn.
S1.quote: I can learn the display, but learning it will not pay rent if the roster loses a day.
fieldNote: Her **new AI learning** requires an offered paid guarded camera trial, not merely her occasional reading of maintenance notices.
The **job fallback** begins after actual hours fall and requires a real safe local posting with adequate pay after travel.

steps.text: Ask union delegate for proposed roster and offered paid guarded camera trial
Learn AI reject screen if paid supervised guarded scrap trial is offered
Apply after cuts to posted safe local production if net base wage covers bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the union that AGI could handle bottling orders in 2028, but the robots that can change caps and clear the belt come around 2031. We need a written staffing plan before a new line is bought.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 63 when those robots reach the physical work. I expect our manual capper shifts to go, and I cannot bridge a long gap on less than a month saved or Dev's variable hours. I have been lying awake about which bill would go unpaid first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would stop the planned kitchen repaint and keep that cash for bills. I would join the union's scheduled meeting to demand paid transition places and written staffing dates. I would enrol in an accepted quality-control certificate only if fees, release hours and supervised guarded bottling practice are funded; after passing and losing hours, I would apply to posted safe local quality jobs if base pay after travel covers costs. If no course place exists, I would search the few posted safe packing jobs on the same pay and shift terms while keeping any paid capper shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. My certificate and years on the line do not turn a lost shift into a retirement income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What practical work should that course include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would reject a leaking cap, record its torque and isolate the capper before clearing a jam. A trainer must watch this on a guarded line, not send me a login for a slide show.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you retire when the robots arrive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if written retirement income and Dev's reliable earnings actually cover housing, food and health costs. We have not checked that sum, and a birthday cannot make it positive.

say: I would ask the **union** for a written pre-2031 staffing plan.
The **2028 planning change** comes before robots handle physical caps.
think: At **63**, lost capper shifts would threaten essential bills.
Less than one month's **savings** cannot fund a long job search.
do: **Cancel** the kitchen repaint and retain money for bills.
**Attend** the scheduled union transition meeting about paid places and staffing dates.
**Enrol** only in funded accepted practical quality training, then apply to posted safe jobs at viable pay.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected major income loss and sleepless bill worries.
S2.quote: My certificate and years on the line do not turn a lost shift into a retirement income.
fieldNote: The **robot date** threatens her physical capper role around 2031 after AGI first changes order planning.
Her **quality and packing routes** both require actual safe local postings with base pay after travel and shifts that cover costs.

steps.text: Cancel planned kitchen repaint and keep cash for bills
Attend scheduled union transition meeting for paid places and written staffing dates
Enrol in accepted quality course only if funded paid supervised guarded place offered
Apply after cuts to posted local quality if qualified or packing otherwise, at bill-covering net pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell our delegate that AGI may plan bottle orders in 2031 while capable robots reach the capper around 2034. Five years gives a union time to negotiate actual paid training seats, provided we begin now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 66 I may still need a wage because our savings are almost nil and we have no verified retirement budget. I have a vocational certificate and average machine skill, but few local bottling posts might remain. Extra time helps only if it leads to a funded course and a real job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would attend the next contract meeting and ask the union to seek paid release and recognised quality places with supervised guard and lockout practice. If an accepted funded place is offered, I would enrol while shifts still pay; after passing, if hours fall, I would apply to posted safe local quality jobs only if guaranteed base pay after travel and shift times covers bills. If no course place opens, I would apply to the few posted safe packing jobs on those same terms, rather than quit the capper early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but the longer notice gives me a chance to press for a paid route. Our bills will not wait for a course brochure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you know the credential is accepted?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would match the course title to the qualification in a real nearby quality vacancy and ask the employer whether the practice counts. If nobody nearby accepts it, the union should ask for a different funded place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the capper meanwhile?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep testing seals and take every paid shift that is safe and offered. The low rate still pays more than a training promise without a place.

say: I would push for **paid course seats** before the 2034 physical robot change.
A **local job advert** should establish which quality certificate counts.
think: At **66**, retirement is unproven against household costs.
Few nearby **bottling vacancies** narrow the fallback from a lost shift.
do: **Attend** the contract meeting to seek paid release and recognised places.
**Enrol** in accepted funded quality training only with supervised guarded practice.
**Apply** after cuts to posted safe quality if qualified, or packing if no place, at workable net pay.
feel: **Anxious** about needing wages at 66 despite longer notice.
S3.quote: Our bills will not wait for a course brochure.
fieldNote: Her **union activity** is a scheduled contract meeting about paid seats, release and safety, not merely personal course research.
She ties **training and both applications** to an offered accepted place or real safe vacancies with guaranteed pay after travel.

steps.text: Attend union contract meeting to seek paid recognised training and release
Enrol if accepted funded paid guarded quality place is offered
Apply after cuts to posted local quality if qualified or packing otherwise, at bill-covering net pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AGI could plan bottling orders in 2036 while capable robots handle the capper around 2039. Ten years is a long time, but we should not spend it pretending a low wage will grow into a retirement fund on its own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 71 at the physical robot date if I am still employed. Dev and I could stop earlier only if written retirement income covers all our housing and health costs; we have not seen those figures. With almost no savings now, I cannot treat the distant date as a promise of comfort.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep taking safe paid capper shifts and request written retirement-income estimates and a full cost list this year. I would ask the union at its next meeting to seek funded paid quality places with supervised guarded practice; if an accepted place is offered, I would enrol. If I still need wages after 2036 and hours fall, I would apply only to posted safe local production or quality jobs whose base pay after travel and shift times cover our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the gap between our current low wage and an unknown retirement income. Ten years gives us time to count, but not money to waste.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What goes on your cost list?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent, food, travel, utilities and likely health costs all go on it beside written income. I would not put our grown children's pay into our household column.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave the capper to take training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only with a real funded accepted place and paid release from shifts. If that place never appears, I keep the wage while it is offered and look at actual safe postings after cuts.

say: I would separate **2036 planning AGI** from physical capper robots around 2039.
A low wage does not guarantee **retirement savings** over ten years.
think: At **71**, I might still need paid work if written income falls short.
Our **thin savings** leave retirement affordability uncertain today.
do: **Keep** safe paid capper shifts and request written retirement figures.
**Ask** the union to seek paid funded guarded quality places; enrol only if accepted.
**Apply** after 2036 cuts if still working to posted safe jobs with viable net pay.
feel: **Anxious** because retirement income remains unmeasured against essential costs.
S4.quote: Ten years gives us time to count, but not money to waste.
fieldNote: Her **retirement request** seeks evidence rather than committing to an early exit; actual income must cover all household costs.
The **training route** remains conditional on a funded accepted safe place and posted work with adequate net wages.

steps.text: Request written retirement income and household cost figures this year
Ask union at next meeting to seek funded paid safe quality places
Enrol only if an accepted funded paid guarded quality place is offered
Apply after 2036 cuts if working to posted safe jobs if net base pay fits

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 AGI and 2031 robot picture is worst because it could remove the capper shifts before Dev and I know whether we can live without them. Written staffing dates, paid guarded quality training that local plants accept, and actual safe job adverts with enough pay after travel would help. Our union needs those terms before the machinery is ordered.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who pays while an older operator learns a new line. Training after an unpaid shift is just another bill with a certificate at the end.

headlineQuote: Training after an unpaid shift is just another bill with a certificate at the end.
portrait: **Priya**, 58, is an experienced mid-level bottling capper operator with a vocational certificate and average machine skill.
She and her **partner Dev** have grown children, lower operator pay, less than one month's expenses saved and few similar local jobs.
She reads **AI notices occasionally** after a mechanic checks them and supports union bargaining for paid safe training and staffing.
Expected **2031 physical robots** threaten essential shifts; any retirement choice needs written income that covers household costs.
biggestWorry: **2031 capper robots** could remove her low-paid but essential shifts before a viable retirement or local job exists.
whatWouldHelp: She needs **written staffing dates**, accepted funded guarded training on paid time and posted safe local work at bill-covering net wages.
